lead: A two-stroke engine has no separate exhaust stroke. The piston must clear burnt gas and fill the cylinder while the ports are open near bottom dead centre. Fresh charge is pushed in by the crankcase pump in small engines or by a blower in large ones. The port layout decides how much charge stays and how much escapes with the exhaust. This chapter defines delivery ratio, trapping efficiency and scavenging efficiency, then compares cross, loop and uniflow scavenging. These ideas appear in scooters, chainsaws, outboard motors and large marine diesels.
prereq: You need: two-stroke engines and port timing diagrams, and the reason a blower raises intake density from Supercharging.

blocks.text: In a four-stroke engine a separate exhaust stroke removes burnt gas. A two-stroke engine has only a short overlap near bottom dead centre. Scavenging is the process of replacing burnt gas with fresh charge during that overlap. The fresh charge is air in a CI engine and air-fuel mixture in an SI engine.

Burnt gas starts to leave when the exhaust port opens because cylinder pressure is above atmospheric. The rest must be pushed out by fresh charge at a slightly higher pressure. Small engines use the crankcase as a pump: the piston downstroke compresses charge in the crankcase, and a reed valve or piston-port skirt controls entry. Larger engines use a separate blower, often a Roots blower.

blocks.where: D is delivery ratio; V<sub>del</sub> is fresh charge delivered per cycle, in cm³; V<sub>s</sub> is swept volume, in cm³.

blocks.text: η<sub>t</sub> is trapping efficiency; V<sub>tr</sub> is fresh charge trapped in the cylinder, in cm³.
η<sub>s</sub> is scavenging efficiency; V<sub>ec</sub> is the total cylinder volume at exhaust closure, in cm³.

Delivery ratio measures how much charge the blower supplies relative to the swept volume. Trapping efficiency measures how much of that delivered charge stays. Scavenging efficiency measures how much of the cylinder contents at exhaust closure is fresh charge. The three are linked by η<sub>s</sub> = η<sub>t</sub> × D × V<sub>s</sub> ÷ V<sub>ec</sub>. When V<sub>ec</sub> is close to V<sub>s</sub>, η<sub>s</sub> ≈ η<sub>t</sub> × D. The product η<sub>t</sub> × D is also called the charging efficiency: trapped fresh charge per swept volume. Strictly, all of these are mass ratios. Volumes can stand in for masses only when every volume is referred to the same pressure and temperature, usually the outside air, and the worked example does exactly that.

Cross scavenging uses transfer and exhaust ports on opposite sides. The piston crown carries a raised deflector beside the transfer port that turns the incoming charge upward, so it rises along the transfer side, crosses under the head and comes down the exhaust side, pushing burnt gas ahead of it. The layout is simple and cheap. But part of the charge still takes the short path straight across: it short-circuits to the exhaust port before it mixes with burnt gas, and the heavy deflector crown runs hot. Short-circuiting wastes air and, in an SI engine, fuel and oil.

Loop scavenging, often called Schnuerle scavenging, angles two transfer ports toward the back wall. The two streams meet, rise along the rear wall, turn across the cylinder head, and sweep down toward the exhaust port. The loop gives better mixing and trapping than cross flow. It uses less air for the same output and has lower short-circuiting. Many small motorcycle and scooter engines use loop scavenging with piston-controlled ports.

A reed valve at the crankcase inlet opens when crankcase pressure falls below atmospheric and closes when pressure rises. A piston-port inlet uses the piston skirt to uncover the inlet. Both act as one-way valves for crankcase pumping.

Uniflow scavenging sends fresh charge in one direction. Inlet ports at one end of the cylinder are uncovered by the piston. Exhaust leaves at the other end through a poppet valve in the head or through ports uncovered by an opposed piston. The flow does not reverse or cross itself. Mixing with burnt gas is low and short-circuiting is small. Uniflow gives the best scavenging efficiency and the highest power per litre of the three layouts.

The hardware is the price. A uniflow engine needs a blower to supply charge above exhaust pressure, plus valve gear or a second crankshaft for opposed pistons. Large marine two-stroke diesels use uniflow with an exhaust valve and a blower. Small cheap engines stay with loop or cross scavenging because the extra hardware costs more than the fuel saved.

spec.aria: Three two-stroke cylinders. Cross: transfer port left, exhaust right, a deflector on the piston turns the charge up and a dashed arrow shows short-circuiting. Loop: ports on one side, the charge loops round the far wall. Uniflow: inlet ports at the bottom, an exhaust valve in the head.

examples.question: A two-stroke cylinder has a swept volume of 300 cm³. The blower delivers 240 cm³ of fresh charge per cycle measured at outside conditions. Trapping efficiency is 0.80. At exhaust port closure the cylinder contents, referred to the same outside conditions, are 300 cm³. Find the trapped fresh charge, the scavenging efficiency and the delivery ratio.
steps: Given V<sub>s</sub> = 300 cm³, V<sub>del</sub> = 240 cm³, η<sub>t</sub> = 0.80, and V<sub>ec</sub> = 300 cm³.
Trapped fresh charge V<sub>tr</sub> = η<sub>t</sub> × V<sub>del</sub> = 0.80 × 240 cm³ = 192 cm³.
Scavenging efficiency η<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>tr</sub> / V<sub>ec</sub> = 192 cm³ / 300 cm³ = 0.64.
Delivery ratio D = V<sub>del</sub> / V<sub>s</sub> = 240 cm³ / 300 cm³ = 0.80.
Check: η<sub>t</sub> × D = 0.80 × 0.80 = 0.64, which equals η<sub>s</sub> because V<sub>ec</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>.
examples.answer: The trapped fresh charge is 192 cm³, the scavenging efficiency is 0.64 (64 percent), and the delivery ratio is 0.80.

examples.question: Two simple models bracket real scavenging. Perfect displacement: fresh charge pushes burnt gas out like a piston, with no mixing, so η<sub>s</sub> = D until D reaches 1. Perfect mixing: fresh charge mixes at once with the whole cylinder contents, giving η<sub>s</sub> = 1 − e<sup>−D</sup>. For the cylinder of the first worked example (D = 0.80, V<sub>ec</sub> = Vs), find η<sub>s</sub> from each model and compare with the 0.64 it achieved.
steps: The cylinder achieved η<sub>s</sub> = 0.64, between the two: better than full mixing, worse than ideal displacement.

Trapping efficiency in each model, using η<sub>t</sub> = η<sub>s</sub> ÷ D: displacement 0.80/0.80 = 1.00 (no charge lost); mixing 0.551/0.80 = 0.69; the real cylinder 0.80. Loop and uniflow designs push a real engine towards the displacement line; cross flow and short-circuiting pull it towards mixing or below.
examples.answer: Displacement gives 0.80, mixing 0.55; the real 0.64 lies between them.

traps: Delivery ratio, trapping efficiency and scavenging efficiency are three different numbers. Delivered volume is not trapped volume, because part of the fresh charge leaves with the exhaust.
Scavenging efficiency uses the cylinder contents at exhaust closure, not the swept volume, unless the question says the two volumes are equal.

Cross scavenging is not loop scavenging. Cross flow has opposite ports and a straight path, so short-circuiting is high; loop flow uses angled transfer streams that meet and turn around the cylinder wall.
Uniflow does not remove the need for a pressure difference. It still needs a blower or pump to drive fresh charge from the inlet end to the exhaust end.
In a crankcase-scavenged SI engine, short-circuited charge carries fuel and lubricating oil, so the lost charge is not just lost air.

quiz.q: Define delivery ratio and write its formula.
quiz.a: Delivery ratio is the fresh charge delivered per cycle divided by the swept volume: D = V<sub>del</sub> / V<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: Name the two hardware arrangements used to obtain uniflow scavenging.
quiz.a: An exhaust poppet valve in the cylinder head, or an opposed piston that uncovers exhaust ports at the other end of the cylinder.

quiz.q: Why does cross scavenging short-circuit more than loop scavenging?
quiz.a: In cross scavenging the transfer port faces the exhaust port, so fresh charge can travel straight across and reach the exhaust before it mixes. In loop scavenging the transfer streams meet and turn along the rear wall, giving a longer path and better mixing.

quiz.q: Why does a crankcase-scavenged two-stroke need a reed valve or a piston-port valve?
quiz.a: The crankcase acts as a pump. The valve lets fresh charge enter the crankcase when pressure is low and closes when the piston compresses the crankcase charge, so charge goes to the cylinder instead of back out of the inlet.

quiz.q: A 250 cm³ two-stroke engine delivers 200 cm³ of fresh charge per cycle. Trapping efficiency is 0.75 and the cylinder volume at exhaust closure is 250 cm³. Find the trapped fresh charge, the scavenging efficiency and the delivery ratio.
Compare a small scooter engine using crankcase scavenging with a large marine diesel using uniflow scavenging. Consider short-circuiting, air used and hardware.
quiz.a: The scooter has simple piston ports or a reed valve and no separate blower, but short-circuiting is higher and some fuel-air charge is lost. The marine diesel needs a blower, an exhaust valve and more hardware, but uniflow flow gives low short-circuiting, low air waste and high power per litre.

quiz.q: Explain why uniflow gives the best scavenging but is not common in cheap small engines.
quiz.a: One-direction flow reduces mixing and short-circuiting, so trapping is high. But uniflow needs a blower plus valve gear or opposed pistons and two crankshafts. That cost is too high for a cheap scooter or chainsaw, where loop scavenging is good enough.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern two-stroke design uses CFD to shape transfer ports and to predict short-circuiting before a casting is made. Large marine engines combine uniflow scavenging with electronically controlled exhaust valves and turbocharging. Small engines use reed valves and stratified (air-head) scavenging, which sends a slug of pure air ahead of the mixture so that what short-circuits is mostly air. Search for 'Schnürle porting CFD' or 'two-stroke scavenging efficiency measurement' to go deeper.
